result.question: Survey what is actually working, right now (2022-2026), to attract interested learners to sign up for email newsletters/mailing lists, and diagnose why some approaches succeed while others fail — across creators, newsletter operators, course-sellers, coaches, consultants, and professional educators — then flag which tactics transfer to a solo B2B expert selling training/thought leadership in the Agile + GenAI space.
result.summary: Strategy: split the question along the evidence bar and the specific sub-questions. One angle chases hard benchmark numbers on opt-in conversion by lead-magnet format; one chases the diagnostic "why PDFs/quizzes fail now" angle; one isolates B2B/expert-led audiences versus consumer creators; one covers the newsletter-first/recommendation-network growth model; and one gathers concrete before/after case studies plus the offer-vs-format mechanism. Together they hit benchmarks, case studies, named examples, and mechanism explanations while keeping recency (2022-2026) central.

results.title: What's The Best Lead Magnet? Analysis Of 41,000+ Forms — MailerLite
results.snippet: Benchmark gold and a direct answer to Mark's problem. Across 41,000+ forms, avg opt-in was 22.16%; a plain 'newsletter/updates' offer was the second-worst performer, while interactive tools (calculators, quizzes, AI generators) hit 26.44%, reports/ebooks 24.61%, checklists 23.22%. Reframes the diagnosis: it's not PDF-vs-newsletter, it's relevance/personalization. Provides the by-format opt-in table the report needs.

results.title: 9 Quiz Funnel Mistakes and How to Avoid Them — ScoreApp
results.snippet: The core 'why quizzes fail' mechanism piece — directly diagnoses Mark's GenAI quiz. Named failure modes: weak landing page kills it before Q1; 5-8 questions is the sweet spot (fewer feels shallow, more drives drop-off after 8-10); asking for email too early; and the biggest under-investment — the post-quiz segmented follow-up. Argues quizzes work because of structured segmentation, not because they captured an email.

results.title: Quiz Funnels vs. PDF Lead Magnets: Which Converts Better? — Brothers Automate
results.snippet: Head-to-head on Mark's two exact tactics. Cites Interact data (80M+ leads) putting quiz conversion ~40.1% vs 5-10% for static pages/gated PDFs, then explains the real difference is data richness: a PDF yields an email; a quiz yields email + 5-7 struggle/readiness data points that power segmented follow-up. Also lists the 'built backwards' failure (collecting data vs transforming how prospects feel).

results.title: Your Lead Magnet PDF Is Dying (and You Know It) — Interactive Lead Gen
results.snippet: Mechanism explanation for why generic PDFs cratered: AI summaries replaced 50-page PDFs, cheat-sheet conversions collapsed as the format feels dated, and vague 'sign up for our newsletter' fails because people don't trust the brand to send useful content. Gives a concrete diagnostic signal — a magnet is failing when downloads are high but replies/business signups are low or unsubscribes spike after the first nurture email.

results.title: Why Your Lead Magnet Isn't Converting (And What To Do Instead) — Phil Smy
results.snippet: Makes the 'specificity of promise beats format' argument central to Mark's fix: a 'Comprehensive Guide' converts <1% because solving everything appeals to no one, while a single-problem, fast-win promise ('the exact email sequence that gets 40% open rates') still converts. Contrasts 'Free guide to grow your list' vs a named 15-minute sequence — 'one feels like advice, the other feels like relief.'

results.title: How Real Lead Magnets Grow Newsletter Lists — beehiiv Blog
results.snippet: Newsletter-operator view (beehiiv era) on pairing lead magnets with newsletter-first growth and why the magnet must match what best buyers actually want, not just rack up raw subscriber counts. Useful for the 'newsletter IS the product' / full-funnel-value thread and connecting the opt-in to downstream business results rather than vanity signups.

results.title: Lead Magnet Conversion Benchmarks 2026: B2B Data Guide
results.snippet: Most relevant to Mark's B2B expert context. Synthesizes ~8 benchmark reports and delivers the crucial methodological caveat: the ~10-20x spread between formats is mostly about who is counted and traffic source, not intrinsic format superiority. Cites Unbounce (41,000 pages, 464M visitors) median landing page = 6.6%; quiz start-to-lead >40%; popups ~4%; email traffic converts 19.3% vs paid social 3.1%. Directly supplies benchmark evidence bar #3 plus the mechanism caveat.

results.title: Lead Magnet Conversion Benchmarks 2026 - Subpage.co
results.snippet: Source of the clean format-by-format table: quizzes 30-40% opt-in with 85%+ consumption; templates/checklists 5-12% (best effort-to-result ratio); ebooks 3-5% opt-in with only 12% consumption. Adds landing-page mechanics (single CTA, specific numbers in headline, 1-2 form fields; >3 fields drops conversion 40-60%). Directly answers the 'rates by format' and 'why PDFs underperform' questions.

results.title: Quiz Funnels vs Lead Magnets in 2026: Which Converts Better
results.snippet: Best for the 'why quizzes work vs fail' mechanism question. Reports quiz opt-in 30-40% vs downloadable guides ~5%, cites TryInteract's 100M+ leads (40.1% quiz average, 65% completion), and is explicit that quiz rates are start-to-lead not visitor-to-lead. Includes revenue-per-lead example ($14.30 quiz vs $4.80 PDF) showing segmentation upside. Vendor-adjacent but transparent about denominator bias.

results.title: Top 20 Lead Magnet Conversion Statistics 2026
results.snippet: Aggregate stat roundup useful for benchmark bar #3. Contains the widely-cited HubSpot 2024 figure that gated ebooks now convert below 0.9% in many sectors while interactive tools exceed 5.2% (~6x gap), plus consumption stats (12% of ebooks finished). Marketing-agency blog, so figures are directional and should be validated against primary reports.

results.title: 18 Data-Backed Lead Magnet Ideas to 10x Your Email List Growth
results.snippet: Covers format choice plus mechanism/positioning: why email/mini-courses feel more valuable than a 'PDF you'll forget,' train open behavior, and why inline placement inside relevant blog posts hits 15-25% (2-3x sidebar). Useful for the 'specificity of promise vs format' and B2B/expert-led transfer questions Mark asked about.

A strong causal claim ("primary reason is X, not Y") is not adequately supported by one conflicted vendor benchmark. Three refutation criteria met: overreach vs. quote, contradicted by independent evidence, and inadequate/marketing source for the claim's strength.
